record.question:
A company connects an on-premises router to AWS through a 200 Mbps hosted Direct Connect connection. A transit virtual interface connects to a Direct Connect gateway associated with a transit gateway. The BGP session is established, the associations are available, and VPC and transit-gateway forwarding routes are correct. However, the on-premises router receives no advertisement for the required VPC CIDR. That CIDR is absent from the Direct Connect gateway association's allowed-prefix list.

Which change addresses the missing route advertisement?

options.text: Enable VPC attachment propagation into the transit-gateway route table and leave the Direct Connect gateway allowed-prefix list unchanged, relying on propagation to advertise the VPC CIDR over BGP.
Add the required CIDR, or an appropriate nonoverlapping aggregate, to the allowed prefixes for the Direct Connect gateway association with the transit gateway.
Upgrade the hosted connection to 500 Mbps because transit virtual interfaces require at least that bandwidth, leaving the prefix configuration unchanged.
Replace the hosted connection with a MACsec-capable dedicated connection and require encryption, leaving the gateway association and prefixes unchanged.
Rotate the BGP authentication key on both ends of the established session, leaving the gateway association and prefixes unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. For a transit-gateway association, Direct Connect advertises the prefixes explicitly configured in the allowed-prefix list. It does not automatically advertise every VPC route from the transit-gateway route table. An aggregate must be appropriate for the intended destinations and must not overlap allowed prefixes of other transit gateways on the same Direct Connect gateway.

<<1>> affects forwarding within the transit gateway but does not populate the separate advertisement list.

<<3>> relies on an obsolete bandwidth restriction. Current documentation permits transit virtual interfaces on dedicated or hosted connections of any speed.

<<4>> changes link encryption and infrastructure, not the missing BGP prefix. Direct Connect MACsec is not configured directly on a hosted connection.

<<5>> changes session authentication. The session is already established, and rekeying does not originate the missing route.

Do not apply virtual-private-gateway semantics here: with a virtual private gateway, the allowed list filters VPC CIDRs; with a transit gateway, the configured prefixes themselves are advertised.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect allowed prefixes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/allowed-to-prefixes.html). [Direct Connect virtual interfaces](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html). [Direct Connect MACsec](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/MACsec.html).

diagram_alt: Direct Connect allowed prefixes originate advertisements for a transit-gateway association, unlike their filtering role for a virtual private gateway.

sources.supports: Transit-gateway association prefixes are explicitly advertised, unlike virtual-private-gateway CIDR filtering.
Transit VIFs support dedicated and hosted connections of any speed; BGP authentication is separate.
MACsec provides link encryption on supported connections and is not supported directly on hosted connections.

editorial_notes: Preserved the repaired answer and current 200 Mbps support; specified a live BGP session and missing allowed prefix to isolate the cause.
